children: India's FX forward premiums extended their post-policy surge to multi-month highs on Thursday on expectations of more central bank sell-buy swaps to drain liquidity, obscuring signals about the rupee's direction.

The one-year implied rate rose as much as 12 basis points to 3.95%, after surging 36 bps on Wednesday following the Reserve Bank of India's policy decision. Shorter-tenor forward premiums hit their highest since April.
The surge, driven by expectations of RBI swaps to drain excess liquidity, has made it harder to judge whether forward rates reflect concerns over the rupee's outlook, traders and analysts said.

"The RBI's use of FX swaps to drain INR liquidity from the banking system is likely to be a double-edged sword. While it does improve the carry on the rupee, it can distort the signal from the FX forward market about the rupee's trajectory," said Dhiraj Nim, an economist and FX strategist at ANZ.

"The market may interpret it as heightened worries over rupee weakness or as an impediment being put up by the RBI to discourage aggressive hedging against the rupee's fall. In the end, drivers of the stress are global, so the worries will linger till they resolve."

The 1-year outright dollar-rupee forward rate moved to 100.5 on Thursday, signalling that markets expect the rupee to breach the key psychological barrier even after the central bank chief on Friday labelled short-term market behaviour irrational and pledged to ensure currency stability.
On the day, the rupee was nearly flat at 96.7675 as central bank intervention helped keep it off record-low levels hit in May.
Higher premiums could spur further importer hedging, bankers said, adding more pressure on the rupee at a time when demand for protection against currency declines is already high.
